Maladaptive Strategies.value: try hard not think about the trauma
Going out at night or being outside after dark
Any form of physical contact with others

Memory.value: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

vignette: Darius was nineteen when the van doors slid shut, sealing him in a windowless space that smelled of damp concrete and old oil. He did not know how long the chains rattled against his ankles or who spoke in the dark, only that the confinement was absolute and the silence between noises was heavier than the metal. When he finally slipped away through a cracked service door, the city air burned his lungs, but the quiet behind his eyes never left. He could not find words to describe what happened to him; the memory sat intact but utterly wordless, a sealed container he refused to open. In the weeks that followed, that wordless knowledge fractured. Sometimes he would feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, a cold dread pooling in his stomach during daylight hours. Other times, specific sounds from the captivity would rise unbidden in his head—metal scraping against stone, a distant mechanical hum—that made him drop his coffee mug or freeze mid-step on the precinct stairs. Because these auditory fragments and wordless surges of panic refused to be ignored, Darius began to systematically close the doors on his own mind. The involuntary memories would flare too suddenly, the mechanical hum growing loud enough to drown out his captain’s briefing, and that relentless intrusion pushed him to make a new rule: he would try hard not to think about the trauma, forcing his attention onto case files and the steady rhythm of the overhead lights. When the sounds returned or the unanchored dread spiked, he could not fight it with logic, so he fled the conditions that invited it. He stopped going out at night or being outside after dark, recalibrating his life around the fading light. He also stiffened whenever anyone reached for his shoulder or tried to pull him close, learning to step back from any form of physical contact with others because proximity felt like the loss of space he had fought so hard to keep. Each recall made the suppression harder, and the avoidance became a necessary shield that he now relied on to function. His role as a detective required him to navigate the precinct’s underground parking garage at dusk to retrieve archived evidence, but the fading light made his pulse spike, so he began delaying every evening retrieval until the morning shift and took long, circuitous routes through the lot. Maya, his girlfriend, noticed how he scheduled their dates strictly before sunset and how he canceled weekend trips that required overnight stays. He did not explain the mechanics of his fear; he simply knew that stepping into the evening meant risking the dark, and the dark meant the box would return in his head. He kept the suppression tight, rerouting his thoughts to traffic patterns, evidence tags, or the hum of the refrigerator when he finally went home. The weight of holding everything down showed in the way his shoulders stayed permanently raised and how he stopped answering non-emergency pager alerts. Six months after the abduction, the walls of his own strategies began to crack during a routine late-night debrief. The fluorescent flicker triggered a sound in his head so vivid he had to grip the table to stay upright. The emotion without image hit him first, a pure, suffocating terror that left him gasping, followed immediately by the wordless knowledge that he was failing to contain it. He had come to believe that letting go meant drowning, but the dampening effect was wearing thin. He booked an appointment not because he had found a way out of the dark, but because the suppression was costing him his sleep, his work, and the steady presence he needed when Maya reached for his. He was hoping for a way to hear the past without the metal scraping, and a way to rest without bracing for the door to open.
